title: Asking politely
job: Requests, thanks, apologies in the right register
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE HONORIFIC RAISES THE SUBJECT, NOT THE LISTENER. -(eu)seyo is -si- plus -eoyo, and -si- honours the person the sentence is ABOUT — so you never use it of yourself. jeo-neun gayo is right; jeo-neun gaseyo is wrong, and it is the mistake an English speaker makes first, because they have learnt -(eu)seyo as "the polite one". L1 shipped five whole phrases containing it — annyeonghaseyo, juseyo, gaseyo, gyeseyo, jinaeseyo — with the rule named as deferred. This is where it becomes productive.

THE REQUEST IS -a/eo juseyo, literally "do it and give it to me": dowajuseyo (please help), gidaryeojuseyo (please wait), sseojuseyo (please write it). L1-M3's juseyo is the second half of every one of them, and each fused form is ONE whitespace token — never hyphenated, because the hyphen in this course marks a particle boundary and nothing else.

jom goes in front of almost any request and is the single most useful politeness word in the language: literally "a little", functionally "please". It softens without changing anything else in the sentence, which is why it is the first thing to reach for and the last thing to leave out.

The softer alternative to a request is an ABILITY QUESTION — V-(eu)l su isseoyo? — which is L1-M6's -l shape doing a new job in front of the noun su, "way" or "means". Asking whether something is possible is less direct than asking for it, exactly as in English, and su is the whole of what is new here.

Thanks and apology finally get their -yo forms, which makes the speech-level decision visible for the first time: gomawoyo is the -yo thanks and L1-M2's gamsahamnida is the frozen formal one; mianhaeyo is the -yo apology and joesonghamnida the formal one, and gwaenchanayo answers both. THE CHIP: a line whose subject is honoured takes formal, plain -yo stays neutral, and informal is NEVER used in this course — the forms that would earn it are banmal, which L1 banned and this level does not lift. The missing value is deliberate.

words.note: Literally 'a little', and it is doing the work English gives to 'please'. It goes in front of the request and softens the whole of it without changing a single other word.

sentences.trap: jom is not asking for a small amount. It is asking gently, and leaving it out turns an ordinary request into an instruction — the one word that most changes how a Korean sentence lands.
sentences.sound: mool jom joo-SE-yo. jom has a short o, closer to English 'jome' than to 'jam'.

variations.changed: without jom, and with the object particle — correct, and much flatter

mistake.why: jom goes next to the verb, not in front of the noun: Mul jom juseyo.

sentences.usage: At any table, any counter, any time you want something handed to you.
sentences.mnemonic: jom is 'a little'. It is also the whole of 'please'.

words.note: dowa- plus L1-M3's juseyo: 'help and give it to me'. Every Korean request is built this way, and the whole of it is one word with no space and no hyphen in it.

sentences.trap: There is no 'me' in this sentence and none is missing. juseyo means 'give it to me' all by itself, so a request built with it already says who the favour is for.
sentences.sound: jom do-wa-joo-SE-yo. Five syllables run together with no break at the seam.

variations.changed: without jom, and it is a real call for help
the ability question, which is softer still

mistake.why: The fused request is one word: Jom dowajuseyo.

sentences.usage: Anything from a heavy bag to a form you cannot read.
sentences.mnemonic: Every request ends in juseyo: do it, and give it to me.

words.note: 'Here', and it takes L1's place particles unchanged: yeogi-e for going or being, yeogi-eseo for doing something here.
anj- plus -euseyo, the honorific ending made productive. It raises the person SITTING, which is why you would never say it about yourself.

sentences.trap: -(eu)seyo honours the SUBJECT of its own sentence. Say jeo-neun anjeuseyo and you have honoured yourself, which is not merely odd — it is the one register error a Korean listener cannot hear past.
sentences.sound: YEO-gi an-jeu-SE-yo. The j of anjeuseyo is soft, and the eu is the vowel with no English equivalent — lips flat, tongue back.

variations.changed: with the place particle, which is equally correct
-eseo, because waiting is something done here

mistake.why: The honorific never lands on yourself: jeo-neun anjayo.

sentences.usage: Offering somebody a seat — in an office, a home, a waiting room.
sentences.mnemonic: The honorific honours the subject. Never yourself.

words.note: The single most useful adverb a learner has, and it is asked for far more often than it is offered. The h in the middle is barely heard.
malsseum is the honorific word for speech — a whole different noun, not an ending — so this raises the speaker in a way malhaeyo cannot.

sentences.trap: malsseum is an honorific NOUN, so the respect is built into the word rather than added to it. Korean does this for a handful of very common things, and asking somebody to speak is one of them.
sentences.sound: cheon-cheon-HEE mal-sseum-HA-se-yo. The double ss is tense, said with the throat tightened.

variations.changed: the adverb on its own request
the request form, which asks a favour rather than instructs

mistake.why: malsseum takes the honorific ending: Cheoncheonhi malsseumhaseyo.

sentences.usage: The sentence that rescues every conversation you cannot follow.
sentences.mnemonic: Some words are honorific all the way through.

words.note: gidaryeo- plus juseyo, the same fusion as dowajuseyo. Waiting is a favour done for the asker, which is exactly what the juseyo half says.

sentences.trap: The -yeo- in the middle is part of the verb and not a separate word. gidaryeo juseyo written apart is understood and is not how it is spelled in this course.
sentences.sound: jom gi-da-RYEO-joo-se-yo. The ryeo is one syllable, said in a single beat.

variations.changed: without jom, and firmer for it

mistake.why: A favour asked takes juseyo: Jom gidaryeojuseyo.

sentences.usage: On the phone, at a counter, in a doorway.
sentences.mnemonic: Wait FOR ME, not just wait.

words.note: sseo- plus juseyo. The tense ss at the front is made by tightening the throat, and it is what separates this verb from a great many others.

sentences.trap: There is nothing here saying WHAT to write, and the sentence does not need it. Korean leaves out anything both speakers can see, which a learner reads as a missing word and a Korean reads as ordinary.
sentences.sound: YEO-gi-e sseo-JOO-se-yo. The ss is tense — the same sound as in masisseoyo.

variations.changed: without the particle, which is how it is usually said

mistake.why: A request takes juseyo: Yeogi-e sseojuseyo.

sentences.usage: Handing somebody a form, or asking for an address.
sentences.mnemonic: If both of you can see it, Korean leaves it out.

sentences.cue: Can you go to Korea tomorrow?

words.note: A noun, not an ending: 'a way'. V-(eu)l su isseoyo is literally 'there exists a way to do it', which is why L1-M3's isseoyo is the verb at the end of it.

sentences.trap: Korean has no verb 'can'. It has a noun meaning 'way' and the ordinary verb for existing, and the two together are the whole of the ability construction — which is why the negative is su eopseoyo, 'there is no way'.
sentences.sound: NAE-il han-gu-GE gal soo i-SSEO-yo. The -l of gal is light, and it runs straight into su.

variations.changed: L1-M9's baeul in the same frame

mistake.why: su follows the -l shape: Naeil hanguk-e gal su isseoyo?

sentences.usage: Asking whether something is possible — which is softer than asking for it.
sentences.mnemonic: There is no 'can'. There is a way, and it exists.

words.note: The -yo thanks, beside L1-M2's frozen gamsahamnida. gomawoyo is warm and everyday; gamsahamnida is what you say to a stranger, an official or a stage.

sentences.trap: gomawoyo and gamsahamnida are two SPEECH LEVELS of the same act, not two words for it. This is the first place the level split is visible, and every -yo form in this course sits on the same rung as gomawoyo.
sentences.sound: ne, go-ma-WO-yo. The wo is one syllable and takes the stress.

variations.changed: L1-M2's formal thanks, a rung up
thanks and the answer to it, in one breath

mistake.why: One level or the other, never both: Ne, gomawoyo.

sentences.usage: Answering a favour that has just been done.
sentences.mnemonic: gomawoyo is warm. gamsahamnida is formal. Same act.

words.note: The -yo apology, and joesonghamnida is its formal twin — the same split as gomawoyo against gamsahamnida, on the other half of politeness.

sentences.trap: mianhaeyo apologises for something small and is not an admission of anything. Korean apologises far more often than English does, and reading it as a confession will make you refuse to say it.
sentences.sound: mi-an-HAE-yo, jom gi-da-RYEO-joo-se-yo. The h in mianhaeyo is almost silent.

variations.changed: the formal apology, to a stranger or an official

mistake.why: The apology is yours, so it never takes the honorific: Mianhaeyo, jom gidaryeojuseyo.

sentences.usage: Buying yourself a moment — the commonest apology there is.
sentences.mnemonic: mianhaeyo for small. joesonghamnida for formal.

words.note: It answers thanks and apology alike, asks whether somebody is all right, and declines an offer. Four jobs, one word, and it is heard constantly.

sentences.trap: gwaenchanayo said with a rising tone ASKS whether you are all right; said flat it says that you are. Nothing in the words distinguishes them, and the tone carries all of it.
sentences.sound: ne, gwaen-CHA-na-yo. The written h is silent, so it runs chan-a-yo.

variations.changed: the same word as a question

mistake.why: The -yo form is gwaenchanayo: Ne, gwaenchanayo.

sentences.usage: Answering an apology, refusing an offer, or checking on somebody.
sentences.mnemonic: One word: it's fine, are you fine, no thank you.

comprehensionPool.cue: Can you go to Korea tomorrow?
